dish:Steak-frites.name: Steak-frites
dish:Steak-frites.text: Born in Paris · Sandwich Croque-monsieur The grilled ham-and-cheese is generally dated to around 1910 on the Boulevard des Capucines, where a Paris cafe put it on the menu as a quick bite for theatergoers and workers. Its name - literally 'crunch-mister' - is folk etymology, a bit of counter humor about what was 'in the gentleman'; an earlier printed mention surfaces in an 1891 review, and Proust name-checks it in 'A l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs' (1919). Try it — Cafe de Flore or Les Deux Magots in Saint-Germain-des-Pres, old cafes that still take it seriously. Born in Paris · Seafood Lobster Thermidor Born in Paris in January 1891, the cognac-and-mustard lobster gratin was named for Victorien Sardou's play 'Thermidor,' which premiered at the Comedie-Francaise that month and was swiftly pulled amid uproar as too critical of the Revolution. A chef - often named as Leopold Mourier - is said to have created it to mark the opening at the restaurant Chez Marie (Maison Maire) near the theater, though some accounts credit the Cafe de Paris or place the invention later. Escoffier had codified a recipe by 1903. Try it — A grand old seafood house like Prunier (16th/8th), or a classic Montparnasse brasserie such as La Coupole (14th). Onglet or bavette seared hard, a raft of thin fries, often maitre d'hotel butter or a peppercorn sauce. The unofficial plate of the zinc counter — and it is judged, always, by the fries. Origin Contested between France and Belgium; a nineteenth-century bistro dish, not haute cuisine (Britannica; Wikipedia).

dish:Baguette de tradition francaise.name: Baguette de tradition francaise
dish:Baguette de tradition francaise.text: By law only flour, water, salt and leaven — no freezing, no additives — which is exactly why it goes stale by nightfall. The 'tradition' is the good one; the plain 'baguette' can be industrial. Origin Paris; the name and recipe fixed by the Decret Pain of 13 September 1993 (Legifrance).

dish:Croissant.name: Croissant
dish:Croissant.text: Lamination — butter folded into dough — is the French contribution. Order it 'au beurre'; the cheaper 'ordinaire' is made with margarine. Origin Austrian, not French: descended from the Viennese kipferl and brought to Paris by August Zang's 1838 Viennese bakery on rue de Richelieu. The Marie-Antoinette story is unsupported (The Local; ICE; Chowhound).

dish:Soupe a l'oignon.name: Soupe a l'oignon
dish:Soupe a l'oignon.text: Onions cooked slowly to bronze, beef stock, a raft of bread and gratineed Gruyere. Peasant economy turned ceremony — long the 4 a.m. cure of market porters. Origin French; by lore the restorative of the all-night workers of Les Halles (the market link is tradition, not documented).

dish:Blanquette de veau.name: Blanquette de veau
dish:Blanquette de veau.text: Veal, cream, a whisper of lemon, button mushrooms and pearl onions. The Sunday dish, not the restaurant dish. Origin French home cooking; 'blanquette' from blanc — the veal is poached, never browned, so the sauce stays pale.

dish:Confit de canard.name: Confit de canard
dish:Confit de canard.text: A pre-refrigeration preservation technique now a bistro staple. Honest to say: it is a guest in Paris, native to the land of cassoulet. Origin South-West France (Gascony), not Paris — duck legs cured and cooked slowly in their own fat.

dish:Jambon-beurre.name: Jambon-beurre
dish:Jambon-beurre.text: Baguette, good butter, jambon de Paris. France's best-selling sandwich — reportedly over three million a day — and a fair test of a boulangerie. Origin Paris; born late nineteenth century among Les Halles workers, on the baguette from the 1920s (Wikipedia; Taste of France).

dish:Croque-monsieur.name: Croque-monsieur
dish:Croque-monsieur.text: Ham and melted cheese bound in bechamel, grilled. Crown it with a fried egg and it becomes a croque-madame. Origin Paris; commonly attributed to a cafe on the Boulevard des Capucines around 1910, and in Proust by 1918 (Devour Tours; Grokipedia).

dish:Escargots de Bourgogne.name: Escargots de Bourgogne
dish:Escargots de Bourgogne.text: The garlic-parsley butter is the whole point; the snail is the delivery vehicle. A brasserie classic in the capital. Origin Burgundy, not Paris — its terroir is east, in the vineyards.

dish:Macaron.name: Macaron
dish:Macaron.text: Two almond-meringue shells, a ganache or jam between. The Catherine de' Medici origin tale is charming and doubtful. Origin Italian almond biscuit by descent; the double-shelled 'macaron parisien' is a twentieth-century Paris refinement credited to Laduree's Pierre Desfontaines (Wikipedia).

dish:Le cafe (express au comptoir).name: Le cafe (express au comptoir)
dish:Le cafe (express au comptoir).text: A small black coffee taken standing at the zinc, faster and cheaper than the terrasse. For decades the weak link in a great food city — until the third wave arrived. Origin The cafe as public institution is Parisian; the espresso itself is Italian by machine.

art:Musee Rodin.name: Musee Rodin
art:Musee Rodin.label: 7th arrondissement
art:Musee Rodin.hook: The 18th-century Hotel Biron sits in roughly three hectares of formal grounds: some 2,000 rose bushes of about 100 varieties frame the house, with gravel walks and clipped box beyond. The Thinker broods on his plinth among the box trees, The Gates of Hell rises at the far end, and Rodin's bronze and marble stand under open sky. Indoors the collection is Rodin's own -- The Kiss, the studies, the Camille Claudel room.
art:Musee Rodin.text: The 18th-century Hotel Biron sits in roughly three hectares of formal grounds: some 2,000 rose bushes of about 100 varieties frame the house, with gravel walks and clipped box beyond. The Thinker broods on his plinth among the box trees, The Gates of Hell rises at the far end, and Rodin's bronze and marble stand under open sky. Indoors the collection is Rodin's own -- The Kiss, the studies, the Camille Claudel room. This is the one everyone means when they say a museum should come with a garden. You can buy a garden-only ticket and spend a whole afternoon walking the rose alleys with The Thinker for company, the golden dome of Les Invalides over the wall. The garden café L'Augustine, the garden cafe-restaurant set within the sculpture park not far from The Thinker (long known simply as the Cafe du Musee Rodin) -- a small interior salon that spills onto terrace tables in good weather, open Tuesday to Sunday. Anchor Hotel Biron, built between 1727 and 1732 to designs by architect Jean Aubert (with Jacques Gabriel); Rodin took studios here from 1908, and it opened as his museum on 4 August 1919.

art:Musee de la Vie Romantique.name: Musee de la Vie Romantique
art:Musee de la Vie Romantique.label: 9th arrondissement
art:Musee de la Vie Romantique.hook: A green-shuttered villa of 1830 reached down a cobbled alley, once the home of painter Ary Scheffer -- rose bushes, clematis and bellflowers around a little glass conservatory. The collection gathers George Sand keepsakes on the ground floor (furniture, jewellery, a cast of her arm) and Scheffer's Romantic canvases upstairs.
art:Musee de la Vie Romantique.text: A green-shuttered villa of 1830 reached down a cobbled alley, once the home of painter Ary Scheffer -- rose bushes, clematis and bellflowers around a little glass conservatory. The collection gathers George Sand keepsakes on the ground floor (furniture, jewellery, a cast of her arm) and Scheffer's Romantic canvases upstairs. It feels like stepping out of the city into a country cottage. Scheffer held his Friday salons in these rooms, and Chopin, Delacroix and George Sand walked this same garden. The house and its tea salon reopened in February 2026 after a refurbishment. The garden café Rose Bakery salon de the, set in the garden's glass greenhouse and on the leafy terrace, serving scones, cakes and savoury tarts; open Tuesday to Sunday through the year. Anchor Hotel Scheffer-Renan, built 1830, the studio-home of Dutch-born Romantic painter Ary Scheffer (1795-1858); free municipal museum.

art:Musee Bourdelle.name: Musee Bourdelle
art:Musee Bourdelle.label: 15th arrondissement
art:Musee Bourdelle.hook: The preserved studios and apartment of sculptor Antoine Bourdelle -- a warren of ateliers opening onto green sculpture gardens where monumental bronzes, Penelope among them, stand among the trees. His great plaster halls are kept much as he left them.
art:Musee Bourdelle.text: The preserved studios and apartment of sculptor Antoine Bourdelle -- a warren of ateliers opening onto green sculpture gardens where monumental bronzes, Penelope among them, stand among the trees. His great plaster halls are kept much as he left them. Bourdelle was Rodin's pupil who became a master in his own right; the permanent collection is free, and after a two-year renovation (reopened 2023) the atelier-gardens are one of the calmest, least-visited corners in the city. The garden café Le Rhodia, the on-site tea room and cafe-restaurant opened in the 2023 renovation, where you can linger over a gourmet menu in the shade of the master's sculptures; the cafes of Montparnasse are also a couple of minutes' walk. Anchor The studio-home of sculptor Antoine Bourdelle (1861-1929), a former assistant of Rodin, who worked here for over four decades; free municipal museum, open Tuesday to Sunday.

art:Musee de Montmartre - Jardins Renoir.name: Musee de Montmartre - Jardins Renoir
art:Musee de Montmartre - Jardins Renoir.label: 18th arrondissement
art:Musee de Montmartre - Jardins Renoir.hook: The oldest house on the hill -- a 17th-century manor -- with three terraced gardens named for Renoir, looking over the Clos Montmartre vineyard. The collection tells the story of bohemian Montmartre: Toulouse-Lautrec, the Chat Noir, and Suzanne Valadon's reconstructed studio.
art:Musee de Montmartre - Jardins Renoir.text: The oldest house on the hill -- a 17th-century manor -- with three terraced gardens named for Renoir, looking over the Clos Montmartre vineyard. The collection tells the story of bohemian Montmartre: Toulouse-Lautrec, the Chat Noir, and Suzanne Valadon's reconstructed studio. Renoir rented rooms here and painted the Bal du Moulin de la Galette and The Swing (La Balancoire) in these very gardens -- you sit where the pictures were made, above the last working vines in Paris. The garden café Cafe Renoir, tucked into the gardens overlooking the vineyard, open Wednesday to Sunday (a 6-euro garden-and-cafe ticket lets you in even without the full museum). Anchor 12 rue Cortot, a 17th-century house; Renoir had a studio here in 1875-1876, and Valadon and Utrillo later worked in the building.

art:Musee Zadkine.name: Musee Zadkine
art:Musee Zadkine.label: 6th arrondissement
art:Musee Zadkine.hook: A tiny house and studio hidden behind the streetfront, entered through a pocket sculpture garden shaded by birch, maple, prunus and Virginia creeper, where Zadkine's bronzes -- Orpheus, the Torso of the Destroyed City -- still stand where he placed them.
art:Musee Zadkine.text: A tiny house and studio hidden behind the streetfront, entered through a pocket sculpture garden shaded by birch, maple, prunus and Virginia creeper, where Zadkine's bronzes -- Orpheus, the Torso of the Destroyed City -- still stand where he placed them. One of the smallest and most secret gardens in Paris; you can genuinely be alone with the sculptures. The permanent collection is free, open daily except Monday. The garden café No cafe on site -- but the Jardin du Luxembourg is a minute away and the cafes of rue d'Assas and rue Vavin are around the corner. Anchor The home-studio of Cubist sculptor Ossip Zadkine (1890-1967), who lived here from 1928 until his death; free municipal museum.

art:Musee Cernuschi.name: Musee Cernuschi
art:Musee Cernuschi.label: 8th arrondissement
art:Musee Cernuschi.hook: A grand 1870s mansion whose windows open straight onto Parc Monceau. Inside is one of Europe's great collections of Chinese and Japanese art -- archaic bronzes, a monumental Japanese Buddha, jades and ceramics.
art:Musee Cernuschi.text: A grand 1870s mansion whose windows open straight onto Parc Monceau. Inside is one of Europe's great collections of Chinese and Japanese art -- archaic bronzes, a monumental Japanese Buddha, jades and ceramics. Here the park is the garden: you leave the Asian bronzes and step directly into Monceau's follies, colonnade and lawns. The permanent collection is free. The garden café No cafe inside the museum; Parc Monceau's benches and kiosks are right outside the door. Anchor The former mansion of Italian-French banker and collector Henri Cernuschi (1821-1896); opened as a City of Paris museum in 1898.

art:Petit Palais (Musee des Beaux-Arts d.name: Petit Palais (Musee des Beaux-Arts de la Ville de Paris)
art:Petit Palais (Musee des Beaux-Arts d.label: 8th arrondissement
art:Petit Palais (Musee des Beaux-Arts d.hook: Charles Girault's 1900 palace wraps around a semicircular arcaded courtyard garden: a gilded peristyle, palms and banana trees, three tiled ponds in blue and gold, mosaic-topped tables. The collection runs from antiquity to 1900.
art:Petit Palais (Musee des Beaux-Arts d.text: Charles Girault's 1900 palace wraps around a semicircular arcaded courtyard garden: a gilded peristyle, palms and banana trees, three tiled ponds in blue and gold, mosaic-topped tables. The collection runs from antiquity to 1900. One of the loveliest free things in Paris -- the permanent collection costs nothing, and the inner garden is a hidden oasis a single step off the busiest avenue in the city. The garden café Le Jardin du Petit Palais, the cafe-restaurant set right in the arcaded courtyard garden beneath the palms (bistronomic menu by chef Amandine Chaignot), open Tuesday to Sunday; reachable even without a museum ticket. Anchor Built by architect Charles Girault for the 1900 Exposition Universelle; a museum since 1902; free permanent collection.

art:Musee Nissim de Camondo.name: Musee Nissim de Camondo
art:Musee Nissim de Camondo.label: 8th arrondissement
art:Musee Nissim de Camondo.hook: A mansion built in 1911-1914 in the manner of Versailles' Petit Trianon, its rear rooms and formal garden opening onto Parc Monceau. Inside, a perfectly preserved collection of 18th-century French decorative arts -- panelling, furniture, Sevres porcelain, silver.
art:Musee Nissim de Camondo.text: A mansion built in 1911-1914 in the manner of Versailles' Petit Trianon, its rear rooms and formal garden opening onto Parc Monceau. Inside, a perfectly preserved collection of 18th-century French decorative arts -- panelling, furniture, Sevres porcelain, silver. A frozen aristocratic house with a heartbreaking story: Moise de Camondo named it for his son Nissim, an aviator killed in the First World War, and left it to the nation; the surviving family was later murdered at Auschwitz. The garden over the park is part of the hush. The garden café No cafe in the house; Parc Monceau lies directly beyond the garden windows for a break. Anchor Hotel Moise de Camondo, built 1911-1914 by architect Rene Sergent with a garden by landscape architect Achille Duchene; opened as a museum in 1936.

art:Grande Mosquee de Paris - tea garden.name: Grande Mosquee de Paris - tea garden
art:Grande Mosquee de Paris - tea garden.label: 5th arrondissement
art:Grande Mosquee de Paris - tea garden.hook: Not a museum but a Hispano-Moorish mosque of the 1920s whose cafe maure opens a tiled patio garden to anyone, no ticket needed -- fig trees, a fountain, blue-and-white zellige, sparrows in the plane trees.
art:Grande Mosquee de Paris - tea garden.text: Not a museum but a Hispano-Moorish mosque of the 1920s whose cafe maure opens a tiled patio garden to anyone, no ticket needed -- fig trees, a fountain, blue-and-white zellige, sparrows in the plane trees. Mint tea poured tall and sweet, gazelle-horn pastries, the shade of the fig trees -- one of the most transporting corners in the Latin Quarter. (A working place of worship with a public tea garden, not a museum in the strict sense.) The garden café The Cafe Maure / salon de the itself, open daily, serving mint tea and North African pastries around the patio. Anchor Built 1922-1926 in Hispano-Moorish style and inaugurated in 1926, raised in homage to the Muslim soldiers who died for France in the First World War.

art:Jardin des Plantes galleries (Museum.name: Jardin des Plantes galleries (Museum national d'Histoire naturelle)
art:Jardin des Plantes galleries (Museum.label: 5th arrondissement
art:Jardin des Plantes galleries (Museum.hook: France's national botanical garden, laid out from 1635, with its long perspective of clipped planes, a rose garden and an alpine garden -- and set within it the museum's great galleries: the Grande Galerie de l'Evolution with its caravan of taxidermy animals under a glass roof, plus mineralogy. (The Palaeontology and Comparative Anatomy gallery is closed for renovation until 2027.)
art:Jardin des Plantes galleries (Museum.text: France's national botanical garden, laid out from 1635, with its long perspective of clipped planes, a rose garden and an alpine garden -- and set within it the museum's great galleries: the Grande Galerie de l'Evolution with its caravan of taxidermy animals under a glass roof, plus mineralogy. (The Palaeontology and Comparative Anatomy gallery is closed for renovation until 2027.) The garden itself is free and open every day; the galleries are the antique heart of natural-history museum-making, and the parade of animals crossing the great hall is unforgettable for children and adults alike. The garden café Les Belles Plantes, the garden restaurant with two large terraces (one over the wallaby enclosure, one shaded by a century-old paulownia), plus a cafe inside the Grande Galerie de l'Evolution. Anchor The Museum national d'Histoire naturelle; botanical garden founded in 1635 as the royal medicinal garden; the Grande Galerie de l'Evolution reopened in its 19th-century building in 1994.

coffee-scene:Belleville Brulerie.name: Belleville Brulerie
coffee-scene:Belleville Brulerie.label: 19th (Belleville)
coffee-scene:Belleville Brulerie.text: The micro-roastery, founded 2013 by Thomas Lehoux, David Flynn and Anselme Blayney, that lit the fuse of Paris specialty coffee and now supplies much of the city (Gault&Millau; Sprudge). Open in Google Maps →

coffee-scene:Ten Belles.name: Ten Belles
coffee-scene:Ten Belles.label: 10th (Canal Saint-Martin)
coffee-scene:Ten Belles.text: One of the original specialty cafes, pouring Belleville Brulerie beans — a template the city copied (European Coffee Trip; Paris by Mouth). Open in Google Maps →

coffee-scene:Telescope.name: Telescope
coffee-scene:Telescope.label: 1st (rue Villedo)
coffee-scene:Telescope.text: Opened 2012 by Nicolas Clerc, a tiny Right-Bank pioneer of the scene, listed by Le Fooding and Paris by Mouth. Open in Google Maps →

coffee-scene:La Cafeotheque.name: La Cafeotheque
coffee-scene:La Cafeotheque.label: 4th (near the Seine)
coffee-scene:La Cafeotheque.text: The earliest of them all, opened 2005 by Gloria Montenegro; the training ground where several later roasters cut their teeth (Sprudge; Paris by Mouth). Open in Google Maps →

coffee-scene:Coutume.name: Coutume
coffee-scene:Coutume.label: 7th (rue de Babylone)
coffee-scene:Coutume.text: Founded 2010-11 by Antoine Netien and Tom Clark, a Left-Bank roaster that brought antipodean coffee culture to Paris (Time Out; European Coffee Trip). Open in Google Maps →

coffee-scene:KB CafeShop.name: KB CafeShop
coffee-scene:KB CafeShop.label: 9th (South Pigalle)
coffee-scene:KB CafeShop.text: Opened 2010 by Nicolas Piegay, named for the Australian kookaburra; an early standard-bearer now with its own roastery (press; specialtycoffee.paris). Open in Google Maps →

coffee-scene:Fragments.name: Fragments
coffee-scene:Fragments.label: 4th (Marais)
coffee-scene:Fragments.text: A serious Marais espresso bar sourcing small-batch roasters; a fixture of the neighbourhood coffee crawl (Time Out; Sprudge; goop). Open in Google Maps →

coffee-scene:Cafe Lomi.name: Cafe Lomi
coffee-scene:Cafe Lomi.label: 18th (La Goutte d'Or)
coffee-scene:Cafe Lomi.text: A northern roastery whose beans turn up across the city, including at Fragments — part of the roaster backbone (Cafe Nuances guide; European Coffee Trip). Open in Google Maps →

bars:Le Verre Vole.name: Le Verre Vole
bars:Le Verre Vole.label: 10th (Canal Saint-Martin)
bars:Le Verre Vole.text: Opened 2000 by Cyril Bordarier, one of the very first caves a manger — a wine shop you eat in — that seeded the whole natural-wine wave (Le Fooding; Club Oenologique; Departures). Open in Google Maps →

bars:Septime La Cave.name: Septime La Cave
bars:Septime La Cave.label: 11th (rue Basfroi)
bars:Septime La Cave.text: The bottle-shop-by-day, standing-bar-by-night offshoot of Bertrand Grebaut's Septime (one Michelin star; World's 50 Best No. 40, 2025) — an epicentre of the modern scene. Open in Google Maps →

bars:La Buvette.name: La Buvette
bars:La Buvette.label: 11th (rue Saint-Maur)
bars:La Buvette.text: Camille Fourmont's tiny former cremerie; a short natural list and a few perfect small plates (giant white beans, cedrat, oil). Paris by Mouth calls it essential. Open in Google Maps →

bars:Le Baratin.name: Le Baratin
bars:Le Baratin.label: 20th (Belleville)
bars:Le Baratin.text: Raquel Carena in the kitchen, Philippe Pinoteau on the cellar for thirty-plus years; the place Paris chefs reportedly drink on their night off (Club Oenologique; PUNCH). Book ahead. Open in Google Maps →

bars:Aux Deux Amis.name: Aux Deux Amis
bars:Aux Deux Amis.label: 11th (rue Oberkampf)
bars:Aux Deux Amis.text: Natural wines chalked on the mirror, rotating small plates; a canonical locals' bar listed by Le Fooding. Open in Google Maps →

bars:Vantre.name: Vantre
bars:Vantre.label: 11th (rue de la Fontaine au Roi)
bars:Vantre.text: A neo-bistro from ex-fine-dining sommelier Marco Pelletier and chef Iacopo Chomel, with a cellar of some 3,000-plus wines; in the Michelin Guide. Open in Google Maps →

gastronomy:Cedric Grolet.name: Cedric Grolet
gastronomy:Cedric Grolet.label: 1st (Le Meurice / Opera)
gastronomy:Cedric Grolet.text: Named World's Best Pastry Chef 2018 by the World's 50 Best; famous for trompe-l'oeil fruit desserts that look exactly like the fruit until you cut them open (World's 50 Best). Open in Google Maps →

gastronomy:Pierre Herme.name: Pierre Herme
gastronomy:Pierre Herme.label: 6th (Saint-Germain, rue Bonaparte)
gastronomy:Pierre Herme.text: The 'Picasso of pastry' (Vogue's Jeffrey Steingarten; La Liste); creator of the Ispahan — rose, lychee, raspberry — and a macaron benchmark. Open in Google Maps →

gastronomy:Cyril Lignac.name: Cyril Lignac
gastronomy:Cyril Lignac.label: 11th and beyond
gastronomy:Cyril Lignac.text: A chef-driven neighbourhood patisserie launched 2011 with Benoit Couvrand (ex-Fauchon); the Equinoxe — vanilla, salted caramel, speculoos — is the signature (press). Open in Google Maps →

gastronomy:Du Pain et des Idees.name: Du Pain et des Idees
gastronomy:Du Pain et des Idees.label: 10th (Canal Saint-Martin)
gastronomy:Du Pain et des Idees.text: Christophe Vasseur, named a top Paris boulanger (2008); the chocolate-pistachio escargot is the pilgrimage pastry (TASTE; AFAR). Open in Google Maps →

gastronomy:Poilane.name: Poilane
gastronomy:Poilane.label: 6th (rue du Cherche-Midi)
gastronomy:Poilane.text: Founded 1932; the two-kilo wood-fired sourdough miche is a Paris institution, not a fashion (Poilane; Wikipedia). Bread rather than pastry, but foundational. Open in Google Maps →

gastronomy:Mori Yoshida.name: Mori Yoshida
gastronomy:Mori Yoshida.label: 7th (avenue de Breteuil)
gastronomy:Mori Yoshida.text: One of the Japanese pastry chefs who reshaped Paris; opened 2013, winner of Le Meilleur Patissier: Les Professionnels 2018 — French classics with precise restraint (Sortiraparis; VisitParisRegion). Open in Google Maps →

natural-wine:Le Verre Vole.name: Le Verre Vole
natural-wine:Le Verre Vole.label: 10th
natural-wine:Le Verre Vole.hook: The cave a manger that wrote the template back in 2000: shelves you drink straight from, and a kitchen (chef Takao Inazawa) built only to flatter the bottle you pull. Book ahead; the room is barely bigger than a living room and you'll know your neighbours by the second glass.

Book ahead; the room is barely bigger than a living room and you'll know your neighbours by the second glass. Signal Open since 2000; owner Cyril Bordarier, chef Takao Inazawa; 400-plus natural references. The format the entire city has been copying for 25 years.

natural-wine:Septime La Cave.name: Septime La Cave
natural-wine:Septime La Cave.label: 11th
natural-wine:Septime La Cave.hook: The little cellar-annexe of the acclaimed Septime, a few doors away. Mostly standing room, cult growers, sharp snacks, plenty of pavement in good weather. Open 4-11pm daily.
natural-wine:Septime La Cave.text: The little cellar-annexe of the acclaimed Septime, a few doors away. Mostly standing room, cult growers, sharp snacks, plenty of pavement in good weather. Open 4-11pm daily. Signal The tiny cave attached to Septime across the street; a fast-rotating list heavy on cult, low-intervention growers (Jura, Rhone, Champagne) rather than a fixed lineup.

natural-wine:La Buvette.name: La Buvette
natural-wine:La Buvette.label: 11th
natural-wine:La Buvette.hook: Camille Fourmont's four-table jewel box: a zinc bar, marinated small things (broad beans with lemon zest, baby octopus), and a small corkage if you pull a bottle off the shelf to drink in. No reservations, so arrive early for a seat.
natural-wine:La Buvette.text: Camille Fourmont's four-table jewel box: a zinc bar, marinated small things (broad beans with lemon zest, baby octopus), and a small corkage if you pull a bottle off the shelf to drink in. No reservations, so arrive early for a seat. Signal Opened December 2012; Fourmont came from Inaki Aizpitarte's Le Dauphin and wrote the 'La Buvette' recipe-and-wine book.

natural-wine:Aux Deux Amis.name: Aux Deux Amis
natural-wine:Aux Deux Amis.label: 11th
natural-wine:Aux Deux Amis.hook: Loud, 70s-neon vintage bistro, by-the-glass list scrawled across the mirrors, superb charcuterie, and a squeeze-in-at-the-bar crush. The rowdy beating heart of the Oberkampf natural-wine crowd.
natural-wine:Aux Deux Amis.text: Loud, 70s-neon vintage bistro, by-the-glass list scrawled across the mirrors, superb charcuterie, and a squeeze-in-at-the-bar crush. The rowdy beating heart of the Oberkampf natural-wine crowd. Signal Small-grower natural list, the owner pouring what he thinks you'll like; open (Yelp updated June 2026).

natural-wine:Vantre.name: Vantre
natural-wine:Vantre.label: 11th
natural-wine:Vantre.hook: An honest hedge: not a natural-wine purist bar but a small bistro sitting on a vast cellar, run by ex-Bristol and ex-Taillevent sommelier Marco Pelletier (chef Iacopo Chomel). Come for the sheer depth of the list rather than low-intervention dogma; there is plenty of living wine among it.

listening:Bambino.name: Bambino
listening:Bambino.label: 11th
listening:Bambino.hook: Tokyo-jazz-cafe spirit in Popincourt: katsu sando and natural wine by day, funk and disco pulled off vinyl by night, and a proper dance floor at weekends. Raw concrete bar, vintage room, high-end rig.
listening:Bambino.text: Tokyo-jazz-cafe spirit in Popincourt: katsu sando and natural wine by day, funk and disco pulled off vinyl by night, and a proper dance floor at weekends. listening:Notre Dame Music Bar.name: Notre Dame Music Bar
listening:Notre Dame Music Bar.label: 11th
listening:Notre Dame Music Bar.hook: A Parisian jazz kissa: full albums played start to finish under low light in a small room, some two thousand records lining the walls, conversation kept low out of respect for the sound.
listening:Notre Dame Music Bar.text: A Parisian jazz kissa: full albums played start to finish under low light in a small room, some two thousand records lining the walls, conversation kept low out of respect for the sound. Signal Vintage McIntosh tube amplification and JBL speakers, a wall of roughly 2,000 records; no reservations, listening first. (Specific turntable/deck models could not be verified and are left out.)

listening:La Recyclerie.name: La Recyclerie
listening:La Recyclerie.label: 18th
listening:La Recyclerie.hook: An eco 'third place' in an abandoned rail station: canteen, an urban farm strung along the old tracks, documentary nights, repair workshops and pop-up markets. Families, ecolos and hipsters share the benches.

listening:Ground Control.name: Ground Control
listening:Ground Control.label: 12th
listening:Ground Control.hook: A former SNCF postal-sorting hall of some 6,500 square metres turned into food courts, bars, galleries and workshops, complete with a grounded aeroplane. Sprawling, festive, genuinely mixed crowd.
listening:Ground Control.text: A former SNCF postal-sorting hall of some 6,500 square metres turned into food courts, bars, galleries and workshops, complete with a grounded aeroplane. listening:La Station - Gare des Mines.label: 18th
listening:La Station - Gare des Mines.hook: Collectif MU's experimental music yard on the ring-road frontier: post-punk, EBM, organic dance and techno, cheap drinks, a scruffy freedom you don't get intra-muros. Honest caveat: it closes 31 October 2026 for a three-year renovation, so catch it while you can.

listening:Le 6b.name: Le 6b
listening:Le 6b.label: Saint-Denis (93)
listening:Le 6b.hook: Six floors of a self-managed creative building out in the banlieue: exhibitions, concerts, a summer beach and a canteen by the water. The suburban counterweight to the inner-Paris scene, and worth crossing the periph for.

around:Giverny.name: Giverny
around:Giverny.label: ~1h15 NW (train to Vernon + shuttle), on the Normandy border
around:Giverny.hook: Monet's house and the Japanese water garden with the lily pond and the green bridge.
around:Giverny.text: Monet's house and the Japanese water garden with the lily pond and the green bridge. The paintings were made here and the garden is the original, replanted each year to Monet's own palette. Season only: open roughly April to 1 November and closed all winter, so plan around it.

around:Auvers-sur-Oise.name: Auvers-sur-Oise
around:Auvers-sur-Oise.label: ~1h N by train (Val-d'Oise)
around:Auvers-sur-Oise.hook: Van Gogh's last chapter: the tiny Auberge Ravoux room where he died, the church he painted, the wheatfields, and his grave beside his brother Theo.
around:Auvers-sur-Oise.text: Van Gogh's last chapter: the tiny Auberge Ravoux room where he died, the church he painted, the wheatfields, and his grave beside his brother Theo. The most concentrated stretch of a painter's final days you can walk in a single afternoon: roughly 70 canvases made in his last 70 days, and the honest, un-touristed melancholy that goes with it.

around:Barbizon.name: Barbizon
around:Barbizon.label: ~1h S, on the edge of the Fontainebleau forest
around:Barbizon.hook: One cobbled street of former painters' studios, the Auberge Ganne where they gathered, and the preserved houses of Millet and Rousseau.
around:Barbizon.text: One cobbled street of former painters' studios, the Auberge Ganne where they gathered, and the preserved houses of Millet and Rousseau. Plein-air landscape painting was effectively invented here in the 1830s, a generation before Impressionism: Millet, Rousseau and Corot fled the city to paint peasants and trees on this exact forest edge.

around:Foret de Fontainebleau & Trois Pi.name: Foret de Fontainebleau & Trois Pignons
around:Foret de Fontainebleau & Trois Pi.label: ~1h S
around:Foret de Fontainebleau & Trois Pi.hook: Twenty-five thousand hectares of oak, white sand and sandstone boulders, with the royal chateau of Fontainebleau at its edge.
around:Foret de Fontainebleau & Trois Pi.text: Twenty-five thousand hectares of oak, white sand and sandstone boulders, with the royal chateau of Fontainebleau at its edge. The oldest and biggest bouldering ground on earth: the 'Font' grade was born here, there are thousands of numbered problems on soft sandy landings, and it is the same rock and dappled light that pulled the Barbizon painters out of Paris.

around:Vaux-le-Vicomte.name: Vaux-le-Vicomte
around:Vaux-le-Vicomte.label: ~55 min SE (near Melun)
around:Vaux-le-Vicomte.hook: The first great collaboration of Le Vau, Le Brun and the gardener Le Notre; candlelit evenings with fountains in summer.
around:Vaux-le-Vicomte.text: The first great collaboration of Le Vau, Le Brun and the gardener Le Notre; candlelit evenings with fountains in summer. The dress rehearsal for Versailles, and honestly the more moving visit: it was so beautiful it got its owner Fouquet arrested by a jealous Louis XIV, who then poached the entire creative team. Far less mobbed than Versailles itself.

around:Chantilly.name: Chantilly
around:Chantilly.label: ~40 min N by train (Oise, just over the regional line)
around:Chantilly.hook: A chateau floating on its own reflecting pond, the Musee Conde old-master collection, and the vast Grandes Ecuries horse museum.
around:Chantilly.text: A chateau floating on its own reflecting pond, the Musee Conde old-master collection, and the vast Grandes Ecuries horse museum. The Conde paintings hang exactly as the last duke willed them: no loans, no rehang, a frozen 19th-century picture gallery often called the richest in France after the Louvre. And yes, the town lays claim to creme Chantilly.

around:Provins.name: Provins
around:Provins.label: ~1h25 SE by train (Seine-et-Marne), UNESCO listed
around:Provins.hook: An intact medieval walled town: over a mile of 12th-century ramparts, the Tour Cesar keep, underground galleries and rose gardens.
around:Provins.text: An intact medieval walled town: over a mile of 12th-century ramparts, the Tour Cesar keep, underground galleries and rose gardens. A survivor of the medieval Champagne trade fairs, preserved in stone rather than restored to look old; the rosa gallica rose trade is woven into the town's identity and its shops.

around:Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pec.name: Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pecheur
around:Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pec.label: ~40 min E by RER, Champigny-sur-Marne (94)
around:Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pec.hook: Across the water to a small island in the Marne (it trades today as 'La Nouvelle Guinguette'): accordion musette, fried fish and white wine under the arbours, salsa on Sunday evenings.
around:Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pec.text: Across the water to a small island in the Marne (it trades today as 'La Nouvelle Guinguette'): accordion musette, fried fish and white wine under the arbours, salsa on Sunday evenings. The living remnant of the riverside guinguettes the Impressionists painted (Renoir's boating-party world). Revived in 1993, it keeps the tradition going literally out on the water, well off the tourist map.

drink:Champagne — grower fizz (the close.name: Champagne — grower fizz (the closest real vineyard to Paris)
drink:Champagne — grower fizz (the close.hook: The grande-marque names on the boulevard ads are blends and marketing, not a place. RM means one family grew the grapes and bottled the wine from its own village, roughly ninety minutes east of the Gare de l'Est — about the nearest true terroir Paris pours. Read the fine print by the cork wire; that two-letter code tells you more than the label ever will.

drink:Chablis & Sancerre — the two bistr.name: Chablis & Sancerre — the two bistro whites by the glass
drink:Chablis & Sancerre — the two bistr.hook: The default un verre de blanc splits two ways. Chablis is chardonnay grown on Kimmeridgian marl — a roughly 150-million-year-old seabed still full of fossil oyster shells — and in its classic village form sees no new oak. Sancerre is sauvignon on Loire flint; that struck-match, gunflint smell has a name, pierre à fusil. Both live or die on a saline, chalky edge, so skip anything buttery or oaked.

drink:Beaujolais — the natural, chilled.name: Beaujolais — the natural, chilled red
drink:Beaujolais — the natural, chilled.hook: Forget the November nouveau; this is serious cru gamay (Morgon, Fleurie, Chiroubles) with little or no added sulphur. It's arguably where the modern natural-wine revival took root in the 1980s, under the influence of the chemist and researcher Jules Chauvet. Ask for it lightly chilled — twenty minutes in the fridge — and the whole-cluster ferment gives that lifted, crushed-cherry rush that makes people drink the bottle too fast.

drink:Cidre & Poiré — the honest outside.name: Cidre & Poiré — the honest outsider
drink:Cidre & Poiré — the honest outside.hook: Honesty first: Paris is not cider country. This is the drink of Normandy and Brittany, and it belongs beside a buckwheat galette, not on a Champs-Élysées terrace. Bordelet, a former sommelier at three-star L'Arpège, makes bottle-fermented cidre that drinks closer to fine wine than beer — look for 'brut' and méthode ancestrale. One thing to know: poiré is pear, not apple.

drink:Pastis — the Marseille drink Paris.name: Pastis — the Marseille drink Paris pours out of habit
drink:Pastis — the Marseille drink Paris.hook: Say it plainly: pastis is Provence and the Vieux-Port, not Parisian terroir — the zinc-bar terrasse serves it on reflex. Cut roughly five parts iced water to one, and watch it turn milky: the anise oils drop out of solution, the louche. That cloud is the whole ritual. (Aside for the curious: Paris does have a licensed still again — Distillerie de Paris, opened 2015 and billed as the first legal distillery in the capital since 1914 — though its output is gin, whisky and rum, not pastis.)

The artisan bottle worth asking for: Henri Bardouin (Distilleries et Domaines de Provence, Forcalquier — up to 65 plants and spices, 45%).

drink:Café crème — the breakfast-only mi.name: Café crème — the breakfast-only milk coffee
drink:Café crème — the breakfast-only mi.hook: The big milky coffee is a morning thing and only a morning thing: order one after lunch and every waiter clocks you as a visitor. Past noon, Parisians switch to un express (a short black) or un noisette (espresso cut with a drop of milk). It is not a cappuccino — no latte art, no oat milk unless you're somewhere new-wave. The teachable half-second: 'un crème', not 'a coffee with milk'.

drink:Coffee — the third-wave espresso.name: Coffee — the third-wave espresso
drink:Coffee — the third-wave espresso.hook: For a century the Parisian petit noir leaned on cheap robusta, roasted near-black and bitter — much of the reason it always seemed to need sugar. Since around 2010 a small wave of roasters rebuilt the cup around single-origin arabica; Belleville Brûlerie (opened 2013, by Parc des Buttes-Chaumont) now supplies many of the city's better bars. Test any café in one question: ask where the coffee is from. A serious one will name the farm.

landmarks:Sainte-Chapelle.name: Sainte-Chapelle
landmarks:Sainte-Chapelle.hook: Louis IX's royal chapel, consecrated on 26 April 1248 and raised in well under a decade to house Christ's Crown of Thorns. The upper chapel's windows rise some 15 metres — roughly 1,113 stained-glass scenes — so that the stone almost disappears and you stand inside a lantern of light.

Signal 8 Bd du Palais, 4e (Île de la Cité). Daily from 9:00 (to 19:00 Apr-Sep, 17:00 Oct-Mar). Since a two-tier fare began on 12 Jan 2026, about EUR 22 for non-EEA visitors and EUR 16 for EEA residents; free for under-18s and EU nationals aged 18-25, and free for all on the 1st Sunday of the month Nov-Mar. Book a timed slot online and expect airport-style security — it shares the gate with the working law courts.

landmarks:Palais Garnier.name: Palais Garnier
landmarks:Palais Garnier.hook: Charles Garnier's opera house, inaugurated 1875 and the temple of Second Empire excess: the marble grand staircase, gilt and mirrors, Marc Chagall's dreamlike 1964 ceiling over the auditorium, and the underground water reservoir that gave Leroux his Phantom.
landmarks:Palais Garnier.text: Charles Garnier's opera house, inaugurated 1875 and the temple of Second Empire excess: the marble grand staircase, gilt and mirrors, Marc Chagall's dreamlike 1964 ceiling over the auditorium, and the underground water reservoir that gave Leroux his Phantom. Signal Place de l'Opéra, 9e. Self-guided daily from 10:00; last entry an hour before the 16:00 close (open to 17:00 from mid-July to end of August). Since 2026, roughly EUR 15 for EEA-resident adults, EUR 25 for non-EEA; under-12 free. Auditorium access is never guaranteed — rehearsals close it without notice. Free audio tour on the Paris Opera app, or simply book a ballet/opera night.

landmarks:Passage des Panoramas.name: Passage des Panoramas
landmarks:Passage des Panoramas.hook: The oldest of Paris's glass-roofed covered passages, opened 1800 — an ancestor of the shopping arcade. The celebrated engraver Stern settled here in 1834 and the storefront survives; today it's a tight run of stamp and postcard dealers and pocket-sized bistros.

The celebrated engraver Stern settled here in 1834 and the storefront survives; today it's a tight run of stamp and postcard dealers and pocket-sized bistros. Signal Entrances at 11 Bd Montmartre and rue Saint-Marc, 2e. Free, open roughly 6:00 to midnight daily. String it together with Galerie Vivienne nearby and Passage Jouffroy directly across the boulevard for an hour out of the rain.

landmarks:Place des Vosges.name: Place des Vosges
landmarks:Place des Vosges.hook: Paris's oldest planned square, completed 1612 under Henri IV (who commissioned it in 1605) — 36 matching pavilions of red brick and pale stone over vaulted arcades, laid out as one of Europe's first pieces of royal town planning. Victor Hugo lived at no. 6 from 1832 to 1848.

The square and its arcades are free and always open; the Maison de Victor Hugo at no. 6 has a free permanent collection, closed Mondays. Bring a picnic from the nearby Marché des Enfants Rouges.

landmarks:Marché des Enfants Rouges.name: Marché des Enfants Rouges
landmarks:Marché des Enfants Rouges.hook: The city's oldest covered market, trading since 1615 and named for a vanished hospice whose orphaned children wore red. Half produce and flowers, half elbow-to-elbow lunch counters — a living market rather than a monument behind glass (listed historic since 1982).

Come hungry and slightly before or after the 13:00 rush; small cash helps at the food stalls.

landmarks:Bourse de Commerce — Pinault C.name: Bourse de Commerce — Pinault Collection
landmarks:Bourse de Commerce — Pinault C.hook: Paris's 18th-century grain exchange under its later iron-and-glass dome — the commodities floor at the edge of Zola's 'belly of Paris', Les Halles — reopened in 2021 as François Pinault's contemporary-art museum, with a raw concrete cylinder dropped inside the rotunda by Tadao Ando.

Signal 2 rue de Viarmes, 1er. EUR 15, EUR 10 reduced (18-26), under-18 free; free the 1st Saturday of the month 17:00-21:00. Open 11:00-19:00, Fridays to 21:00, closed Tuesdays. E. Dehillerin is a two-minute walk — pair the art with the copper.

rooftops:Le Rooftop, Terrass'' Hotel.name: Le Rooftop, Terrass'' Hotel
rooftops:Le Rooftop, Terrass'' Hotel.label: Montmartre
rooftops:Le Rooftop, Terrass'' Hotel.hook: Seventh-floor bar on the Montmartre slope, looking out over a sea of zinc roofs with the Eiffel Tower, Les Invalides and the Grand Palais lined up beyond the graves of Montmartre Cemetery at your feet. The rare panorama you can keep in January.

Signal Open year-round and heated and coverable when the weather turns, unlike nearly every other rooftop in this city; in winter it plays chalet, raclette and all. No reservation, but come outside 7-8:30pm to skip the queue.

rooftops:Le Perchoir Ménilmontant.name: Le Perchoir Ménilmontant
rooftops:Le Perchoir Ménilmontant.label: Ménilmontant
rooftops:Le Perchoir Ménilmontant.hook: The rooftop that started the whole Paris fashion, seven floors up an old industrial building in the working east, with the Vecchio restaurant a level below the bar. Sunset over the Paris the postcards leave out.
rooftops:Le Perchoir Ménilmontant.text: The rooftop that started the whole Paris fashion, seven floors up an old industrial building in the working east, with the Vecchio restaurant a level below the bar. Its Marais sibling atop BHV has closed (now Terraza Mikuna) - this Ménilmontant original is the one that survived.

rooftops:The rooftop terrace, Galeries L.name: The rooftop terrace, Galeries Lafayette
rooftops:The rooftop terrace, Galeries L.label: Chaussée-d'Antin
rooftops:The rooftop terrace, Galeries L.hook: An open terrace on the top floor above the store's Art Nouveau glass dome, offering a free 360-degree sweep from the Opéra Garnier to Sacré-Cœur to the Eiffel Tower. Julien Sebbag's Balcon, which replaced the vegetarian Créatures in May 2026, is there if you want a table.

rooftops:Perruche.name: Perruche
rooftops:Perruche.label: Printemps Haussmann
rooftops:Perruche.hook: Ninth-floor bar-restaurant on the roof of the Printemps men's store, a green tangle of exotic plants over the rooftops, cooking the south - pissaladière, farcis, salade niçoise. Named after the parakeet.

Signal Opens at lunch, unusual for a Paris rooftop, so it works as a rare midday Provençal table with a view - but it also runs late with live music at night, so it is not the quiet option after dark.

rooftops:Le Bar à Bulles.name: Le Bar à Bulles
rooftops:Le Bar à Bulles.label: Pigalle / Blanche
rooftops:Le Bar à Bulles.hook: A hidden green terrace on the third floor of La Machine du Moulin Rouge, tucked behind the windmill's sails at 4 bis Cité Véron, all climbing plants and salvaged vintage furniture. In high summer it screens free open-air films under the stars.

Weekend brunch is a set menu (around 29 euros); the summer film nights are free but need booking.

rooftops:Bonnie.name: Bonnie
rooftops:Bonnie.label: SO/ Paris
rooftops:Bonnie.hook: Sixteen floors up the reinvented Morland tower on the Seine, a fully glassed-in rooftop where a mirrored ceiling turns the river upside down above your head, with the Eiffel Tower, Panthéon and Notre-Dame ringed around.
