Signal A Paris Society restaurant-bar-club: dressy, expensive, reservation-led. But it is the only entirely glassed-in rooftop in town, so it holds up on a grey or cold night when the others shut.

rooftops:Le Tout-Paris.name: Le Tout-Paris
rooftops:Le Tout-Paris.label: Cheval Blanc
rooftops:Le Tout-Paris.hook: Seventh-floor terrace of the Cheval Blanc hotel, tree-lined nooks above the Seine running from Notre-Dame to the Eiffel Tower, with William Bequin's refined brasserie cooking under Arnaud Donckele's watch. It holds one Michelin star.
rooftops:Le Tout-Paris.text: Seventh-floor terrace of the Cheval Blanc hotel, tree-lined nooks above the Seine running from Notre-Dame to the Eiffel Tower, with William Bequin's refined brasserie cooking under Arnaud Donckele's watch. It holds one Michelin star. Signal The splurge tier, plainly. Book the restaurant; or perch at the bar for a single cocktail if the full meal isn't the plan.

rooftops:Les Ombres.name: Les Ombres
rooftops:Les Ombres.label: Musée du quai Branly
rooftops:Les Ombres.hook: Jean Nouvel's all-glass rooftop restaurant on the quai Branly museum, so close to the Eiffel Tower that its iron lace lays a shadow across your table by day and lights the room gold at night; the ceiling turns starry on the hour after dark.
rooftops:Les Ombres.text: Jean Nouvel's all-glass rooftop restaurant on the quai Branly museum, so close to the Eiffel Tower that its iron lace lays a shadow across your table by day and lights the room gold at night; the ceiling turns starry on the hour after dark. Signal A proper sit-down restaurant, not a drop-in bar - reserve, and ask for a terrace table facing the tower. The view is the entire proposition, and the bill says so.

rooftops:Rooftop, Hôtel Dame des Arts.name: Rooftop, Hôtel Dame des Arts
rooftops:Rooftop, Hôtel Dame des Arts.label: Latin Quarter
rooftops:Rooftop, Hôtel Dame des Arts.hook: A 360-degree roof over the Left Bank - Notre-Dame close below, Sacré-Cœur and Montmartre one way, La Défense on the horizon the other - built around Italian aperitivo, negroni and antipasti and the art of doing nothing.
rooftops:Rooftop, Hôtel Dame des Arts.text: A 360-degree roof over the Left Bank - Notre-Dame close below, Sacré-Cœur and Montmartre one way, La Défense on the horizon the other - built around Italian aperitivo, negroni and antipasti and the art of doing nothing. Signal Seasonal, roughly spring to autumn, and reservation-only when busy; one of the few genuine rooftops on the Left Bank, where most of them cluster across the river.

rooftops:Le Rooftop, Molitor.name: Le Rooftop, Molitor
rooftops:Le Rooftop, Molitor.label: Auteuil
rooftops:Le Rooftop, Molitor.hook: The roof of the reborn 1929 Molitor swimming-club hotel out in the far west, looking straight down onto the celebrated open-air pool in its courtyard and out to the Eiffel Tower, cooking the Mediterranean.
rooftops:Le Rooftop, Molitor.text: The roof of the reborn 1929 Molitor swimming-club hotel out in the far west, looking straight down onto the celebrated open-air pool in its courtyard and out to the Eiffel Tower, cooking the Mediterranean. Signal Open May to September only, and it draws a hotel-and-booking crowd out by Roland-Garros and the Parc des Princes - far from the centre, worth the trek for the pool-and-skyline oddity.

linger:Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu.name: Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu
linger:Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu.label: Bourse / Richelieu
linger:Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu.hook: The most beautiful free reading room in Paris: a vast oval hall under a glazed dome, holding some 20,000 open-access books (9,000 of them comics) and 160 seats where anyone at all can sit and work the whole day.
linger:Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu.text: The most beautiful free reading room in Paris: a vast oval hall under a glazed dome, holding some 20,000 open-access books (9,000 of them comics) and 160 seats where anyone at all can sit and work the whole day. Signal Free, no library card, no appointment for the Oval Room - just walk in, sign the Wi-Fi policy, and stay until closing. Closed Mondays. The one grand room in the city that asks nothing of you.

linger:Bibliothèque Mazarine.name: Bibliothèque Mazarine
linger:Bibliothèque Mazarine.label: Institut de France
linger:Bibliothèque Mazarine.hook: The oldest public library in France, Cardinal Mazarin's own collection opened to scholars in 1643, its bust-lined seventeenth-century hall on the Seine still a working reading room, not a museum piece.
linger:Bibliothèque Mazarine.text: The oldest public library in France, Cardinal Mazarin's own collection opened to scholars in 1643, its bust-lined seventeenth-century hall on the Seine still a working reading room, not a museum piece. Signal Free, but you show ID and are issued a reader's pass on the spot before you can settle in to work; closed annually 1-15 August. Expect a scholar's silence, not a café hum.

linger:Bpi, Lumière building.name: Bpi, Lumière building
linger:Bpi, Lumière building.label: Bercy / Terroirs de France
linger:Bpi, Lumière building.hook: The Centre Pompidou's huge public library, decamped for 2025-2030 to a glass building at 40 avenue des Terroirs de France while Beaubourg is gutted; over 8,000 square metres of free desks, Wi-Fi and open stacks across two floors.
linger:Bpi, Lumière building.text: The Centre Pompidou's huge public library, decamped for 2025-2030 to a glass building at 40 avenue des Terroirs de France while Beaubourg is gutted; over 8,000 square metres of free desks, Wi-Fi and open stacks across two floors. Signal Free and built for the long haul, but be clear-eyed: it is no longer the Pompidou or its view, just a functional research library in the 12th. The Centre itself is shut until 2030, so don't turn up at Beaubourg expecting either.

linger:Café de Flore.name: Café de Flore
linger:Café de Flore.label: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
linger:Café de Flore.hook: The 1887 café where Sartre and Beauvoir sat out the war in the warmth and James Baldwin wrote much of Go Tell It on the Mountain upstairs over cognac and coffee. Red banquettes, marble, mirrors - unchanged, on purpose.
linger:Café de Flore.text: The 1887 café where Sartre and Beauvoir sat out the war in the warmth and James Baldwin wrote much of Go Tell It on the Mountain upstairs over cognac and coffee. Red banquettes, marble, mirrors - unchanged, on purpose. Signal Touristy and dear; a small coffee costs what a full lunch does elsewhere. But the quieter first floor is where you actually linger, and once, for the ghosts, it earns the price.

linger:Les Deux Magots.name: Les Deux Magots
linger:Les Deux Magots.label: Place Saint-Germain-des-Prés
linger:Les Deux Magots.hook: Trading as a café since 1884, named for the two carved Chinese figures - the magots - perched on a pillar inside, gazing down over the room; Hemingway, Beauvoir and the Surrealists were regulars. Live jazz on Thursday evenings.
linger:Les Deux Magots.text: Trading as a café since 1884, named for the two carved Chinese figures - the magots - perched on a pillar inside, gazing down over the room; Hemingway, Beauvoir and the Surrealists were regulars. Live jazz on Thursday evenings. Signal Flore's next-door rival and just as expensive; take a terrace table facing Saint-Germain-des-Prés, the oldest church in Paris, and nurse a single drink - no waiter will ever hurry you off it.

linger:Le Select.name: Le Select
linger:Le Select.label: Montparnasse
linger:Le Select.hook: The 1923 café Hemingway called 'the soul of Montparnasse,' once open around the clock, still running past midnight with black-and-white waiters and marble tables you can hold for hours.
linger:Le Select.text: The 1923 café Hemingway called 'the soul of Montparnasse,' once open around the clock, still running past midnight with black-and-white waiters and marble tables you can hold for hours. Signal The least gentrified of the Montparnasse legends - a genuine neighbourhood brasserie rather than a museum. Come late, when it keeps going long after the tourist cafés have shuttered.

linger:La Caféothèque.name: La Caféothèque
linger:La Caféothèque.label: Hôtel de Ville / riverside
linger:La Caféothèque.hook: A rambling coffee 'temple' a block off the Seine, opened in 2005 by a former Guatemalan ambassador, with its own roastery and a long rotation of single-origin coffees - no blends - and worn armchairs made for sinking in with a cup and a book.
linger:La Caféothèque.text: A rambling coffee 'temple' a block off the Seine, opened in 2005 by a former Guatemalan ambassador, with its own roastery and a long rotation of single-origin coffees - no blends - and worn armchairs made for sinking in with a cup and a book. Signal One of the roasters that taught Paris to take coffee seriously; calm and unhurried, though it closes by early evening. Come for the coffee first and the laptop second.

linger:Shakespeare and Company Café.name: Shakespeare and Company Café
linger:Shakespeare and Company Café.label: Latin Quarter
linger:Shakespeare and Company Café.hook: The specialty-coffee annex beside the famous English-language bookshop, facing Notre-Dame across its small square, pouring flat whites and anglo vegetarian plates since 2015.
linger:Shakespeare and Company Café.text: The specialty-coffee annex beside the famous English-language bookshop, facing Notre-Dame across its small square, pouring flat whites and anglo vegetarian plates since 2015. Signal Tiny and often full - far better for a coffee with a newly bought book than a half-day of work. The cathedral framed in the window is the reason to keep your seat while you can.

linger:Le Pavillon des Canaux.name: Le Pavillon des Canaux
linger:Le Pavillon des Canaux.label: Bassin de la Villette
linger:Le Pavillon des Canaux.hook: A former canal-inspector's house on the water, opened in 2014 as half-café, half-coworking room: work in a former bedroom, or literally in a bathtub, over locally roasted coffee with the Bassin de la Villette out the window.
linger:Le Pavillon des Canaux.text: A former canal-inspector's house on the water, opened in 2014 as half-café, half-coworking room: work in a former bedroom, or literally in a bathtub, over locally roasted coffee with the Bassin de la Villette out the window. Signal Genuinely built for working - laptops welcome by day, Wi-Fi that holds, open to midnight (1am Thursday to Saturday) - though not every room allows them. The most unpretentious work spot on this list.

linger:Café Craft.name: Café Craft
linger:Café Craft.label: Canal Saint-Martin
linger:Café Craft.hook: A café designed from the studs up for people who came to work: long communal tables, an outlet at every seat, steady Wi-Fi and a calm room of designers, coders and writers near the canal.
linger:Café Craft.text: A café designed from the studs up for people who came to work: long communal tables, an outlet at every seat, steady Wi-Fi and a calm room of designers, coders and writers near the canal. Signal Here the laptop is the norm, not something merely tolerated - the honest choice when a grand café would quietly resent you. You pay café prices for a desk you can keep all afternoon.

linger:Ten Belles.name: Ten Belles
linger:Ten Belles.label: Canal Saint-Martin
linger:Ten Belles.hook: A pocket-sized specialty roaster and sourdough bakery just off the canal, pouring some of the best flat whites in the city since 2012 from a counter locals actually queue at.
linger:Ten Belles.text: A pocket-sized specialty roaster and sourdough bakery just off the canal, pouring some of the best flat whites in the city since 2012 from a counter locals actually queue at. Signal Too small to camp in - take a sharp coffee and a slice of bread, then a bench by the water. Superb coffee, wrong room for a long session; be honest with yourself about which you need.

linger:Anticafé.name: Anticafé
linger:Anticafé.label: Louvre / Beaubourg and five more
linger:Anticafé.hook: The pay-for-time coworking café: about 5 euros an hour - the tab auto-caps around 24 euros for a full day - buys unlimited coffee, snacks, fast Wi-Fi and a seat you are meant to keep, with a small library and board games for the breaks.
linger:Anticafé.text: The pay-for-time coworking café: about 5 euros an hour - the tab auto-caps around 24 euros for a full day - buys unlimited coffee, snacks, fast Wi-Fi and a seat you are meant to keep, with a small library and board games for the breaks. Signal The guilt-free answer to Parisian laptop-wariness - you are paying for the time, not the coffee. Seven branches across the city; reserve ahead for groups of four or more.

quartiers:Place des Vosges.name: Place des Vosges
quartiers:Place des Vosges.hook: Paris's oldest planned square: a perfect 140m x 140m of matching red-brick-and-stone pavilions raised over vaulted arcades, wrapped around a garden of clipped limes and four fountains. Victor Hugo's apartment at No. 6 is now a museum whose permanent collection is free to visit.
quartiers:Place des Vosges.text: Paris's oldest planned square: a perfect 140m x 140m of matching red-brick-and-stone pavilions raised over vaulted arcades, wrapped around a garden of clipped limes and four fountains. Victor Hugo's apartment at No. 6 is now a museum whose permanent collection is free to visit. Born in Paris · Sauce Sauce Bearnaise Credited to chef Jean-Louis-Francois Collinet, who is said to have served it at the 1836 opening of Le Pavillon Henri IV, a restaurant in Saint-Germain-en-Laye just west of Paris - reportedly a happy accident while working a shallot-and-butter emulsion off a broken hollandaise. He named it for Bearn, birthplace of Henri IV, whose former residence housed the restaurant. The accident tale is the traditional account rather than documented fact, and a similar recipe is said to predate 1836. Try it — Le Pavillon Henri IV in Saint-Germain-en-Laye (the origin site, still a hotel-restaurant); in Paris, order it alongside an entrecote at any classic bistro. A little Paris beauty · Cafe Le Procope Opened in 1686 by the Sicilian Procopio Cutò, who fitted his rooms with crystal chandeliers, wall mirrors and marble-topped tables — the template every European café would copy — Le Procope claims to be the oldest café in Paris. La Fontaine, Voltaire, Diderot's Encyclopédistes and later Danton and Franklin argued over coffee and ice cream here. Honest footnote: the original café shut in 1872 and the space reopened as a restaurant in 1957, so it is a restored shrine to the ritual rather than an unbroken 340-year pour. Where — 13 rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie, 6th arrondissement (also reachable through the Cour du Commerce Saint-André) It stands on grief. Here rose the Hôtel des Tournelles, the royal palace where Henri II died in 1559 after a lance splinter drove through his visor at a tournament; his widow Catherine de' Medici had the whole thing torn down. Henri IV built the square on the cleared ground from 1605 to 1612 and did something no French king had done before: he dictated that every house-front obey a single design, inventing the 'place royale'. It was inaugurated in 1612 with a carrousel for the boy Louis XIII's betrothal to Anne of Austria, and kept the name Place Royale until 1800, when it was renamed for the Vosges department, the first to remit its taxes to the young Republic. Signal built 1605-1612 by Henri IV, renamed Place des Vosges in 1800

quartiers:Place Dauphine.name: Place Dauphine
quartiers:Place Dauphine.hook: A hushed, leaf-shaded triangle of brick-and-stone houses hidden at the western prow of the island, one of the quietest addresses in the middle of Paris.
quartiers:Place Dauphine.text: A hushed, leaf-shaded triangle of brick-and-stone houses hidden at the western prow of the island, one of the quietest addresses in the middle of Paris. Henri IV's second royal square, and the reason it is a triangle and not a rectangle is honest geography: it fills the raw silt-spit at the tip of the Île de la Cité, just off his new Pont Neuf. On 10 March 1607 he handed roughly three acres to Achille de Harlay with a single condition, that every facade repeat the same model, and named the ensemble for the Dauphin, his six-year-old son and future Louis XIII. The last house was finished in 1616. Much altered since, but the triangle and its calm survive. Signal begun 1607 by Henri IV, houses completed by 1616

quartiers:Place des Victoires.name: Place des Victoires
quartiers:Place des Victoires.hook: A circular royal square, now ringed by fashion houses, with an equestrian Louis XIV rearing at its centre.
quartiers:Place des Victoires.text: A circular royal square, now ringed by fashion houses, with an equestrian Louis XIV rearing at its centre. The only one of the great royal squares built not by a king but by a courtier's flattery. Maréchal de la Feuillade commissioned a gilded statue of Louis XIV after the Treaty of Nijmegen, then hired Jules Hardouin-Mansart to raise an entire round square around it (1685-86). The radius was set by the statue's own proportions, and the approaching streets were deliberately kept out of alignment so the king's effigy would always stand clear against the facades. What you teach a visitor here: the original — a standing figure of the king crowned by Victory, not a horseman — was melted down in the Revolution; the equestrian statue there today is Bosio's replacement of 1822. Signal designed 1685-1686 by Hardouin-Mansart, inaugurated by the Dauphin (standing in for the absent king) March 1686

quartiers:Le Marais.name: Le Marais
quartiers:Le Marais.hook: A dense weave of medieval lanes and Renaissance mansions (hôtels particuliers), the Jewish Pletzl around Rue des Rosiers, the Carnavalet and Picasso museums, and the city's oldest cafe-lined stone.
quartiers:Le Marais.text: A dense weave of medieval lanes and Renaissance mansions (hôtels particuliers), the Jewish Pletzl around Rue des Rosiers, the Carnavalet and Picasso museums, and the city's oldest cafe-lined stone. The name means marsh, and that is literal: low, wet ground drained from the 12th century onward by the Knights Templar (Louis VII granted them the land in 1139) and religious orders. It turned aristocratic the moment Place des Vosges opened in 1612, then emptied when the court decamped to Versailles, and decayed for two centuries. The paradox that saved it: too poor to be worth demolishing, its 17th-century mansions were still standing when André Malraux made the Marais France's first protected 'secteur sauvegardé' in 1964. Signal marsh drained from 1139, France's first protected heritage sector 1964

quartiers:Canal Saint-Martin.name: Canal Saint-Martin
quartiers:Canal Saint-Martin.hook: A 4.5km canal of nine locks, arched iron footbridges and plane trees, its quays now lined with bistros and booksellers.
quartiers:Canal Saint-Martin.text: A 4.5km canal of nine locks, arched iron footbridges and plane trees, its quays now lined with bistros and booksellers. Napoleon ordered it dug in 1802 and paid for it with a tax on wine, for a blunt reason: to pipe clean water into a city dying of cholera and dysentery, and to float in grain and stone. It was finished in 1825; Napoleon III later roofed over nearly half of it to lay boulevards on top. The still green water and the swing-bridges are the ones Amelie skips stones across in the 2001 film, and the Hotel du Nord still standing on the quay gave French cinema its immortal cry of 'Atmosphere!' in 1938. Signal ordered by Napoleon 1802, completed 1825

quartiers:Montmartre & the Butte.name: Montmartre & the Butte
quartiers:Montmartre & the Butte.hook: Paris's high point at 130m, crowned by the white domes of Sacre-Coeur, laced with stairs and the Clos Montmartre — the city's most famous surviving vineyard, replanted by the City of Paris in 1933 — above the tourist easels of Place du Tertre.
quartiers:Montmartre & the Butte.text: Paris's high point at 130m, crowned by the white domes of Sacre-Coeur, laced with stairs and the Clos Montmartre — the city's most famous surviving vineyard, replanted by the City of Paris in 1933 — above the tourist easels of Place du Tertre. A martyr's hill: Saint Denis, first bishop of Paris, was said to be beheaded here around 250 AD, giving Mont des Martyrs its name. It stayed a village of gypsum quarries and vineyards until Paris annexed it in 1860, and its cheap rents then drew Renoir, Toulouse-Lautrec, Picasso and Van Gogh. Sacre-Coeur was begun in 1875 as national penance for the defeat by Prussia and the bloodshed of the Commune. One real thing to know: 'plaster of Paris' is Montmartre gypsum, quarried out of this very hill until the mines wound down around annexation. Signal annexed to Paris 1860, Sacre-Coeur begun 1875

quartiers:Belleville.name: Belleville
quartiers:Belleville.hook: A steep, gloriously multi-ethnic working-class quarter climbing above the city, with a Chinatown, North African and Jewish shops, dense street art, and the terraced Parc de Belleville.
quartiers:Belleville.text: A steep, gloriously multi-ethnic working-class quarter climbing above the city, with a Chinatown, North African and Jewish shops, dense street art, and the terraced Parc de Belleville. Once a village of vineyards and open-air guinguettes, it was annexed in 1860 and promptly filled with the workers Haussmann's demolitions had pushed out of central Paris, then wave after wave of immigrants. Edith Piaf grew up singing in these streets; legend has her born under a lamppost on Rue de Belleville in 1915, though the honest record puts her birth at the Hôpital Tenon nearby. The reward for the climb: the terrace of Parc de Belleville, opened 1988 on the neighbourhood's 108m hill, is one of the highest free viewpoints in Paris. Signal annexed 1860, Piaf born in the quarter 1915, park terrace opened 1988

quartiers:Saint-Germain-des-Prés.name: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
quartiers:Saint-Germain-des-Prés.hook: The Left Bank's literary heart: the oldest church in Paris, the terraces of Cafe de Flore and Les Deux Magots, and the publishing houses that still cluster the surrounding streets.
quartiers:Saint-Germain-des-Prés.text: The Left Bank's literary heart: the oldest church in Paris, the terraces of Cafe de Flore and Les Deux Magots, and the publishing houses that still cluster the surrounding streets. It grew around an abbey founded in the 6th century by Childebert I, son of Clovis, to shelter relics he brought back from the siege of Zaragoza — a fragment of the True Cross and Saint Vincent's tunic; the church was dedicated in 558, the very year the king died (23 December), and it became the burial place of the Merovingian dynasty. Fourteen centuries later its cafes became the headquarters of Sartre, de Beauvoir and post-war existentialism. What visitors miss: long before it was a philosophers' salon, the abbey's annual fair made this one of the great marketplaces of medieval Europe. Signal abbey founded c.543-558 (church dedicated 558), existentialist heyday 1940s-50s

culture:Musée de la Vie Romantique.name: Musée de la Vie Romantique
culture:Musée de la Vie Romantique.hook: A green-shuttered 1830 villa at the end of a cobbled courtyard, once a painter's house, now a museum of the Romantic era — with a rose-garden tea salon.
culture:Musée de la Vie Romantique.text: A green-shuttered 1830 villa at the end of a cobbled courtyard, once a painter's house, now a museum of the Romantic era — with a rose-garden tea salon. This was the home of the Dutch-born Romantic painter Ary Scheffer, who moved to rue Chaptal in 1830 and, with his household, held Friday-evening salons that drew the whole 'Nouvelle Athènes' quarter — Chopin, Delacroix, Pauline Viardot and George Sand, who lived minutes away. Sand never lived here but came often, and the museum keeps her jewellery, plaster casts and mementoes. It reopened on 14 February 2026 after a restoration begun in September 2024. One real thing: the garden tea salon is a secret to Parisians, open without a museum ticket, not just a museum add-on. Signal Ary Scheffer's 1830 house; reopened 14 February 2026 after restoration

culture:Musée Gustave Moreau.name: Musée Gustave Moreau
culture:Musée Gustave Moreau.hook: The house-and-studio the Symbolist painter Gustave Moreau turned into his own museum, crammed with some 1,300 paintings, watercolours and drawings and reached by a theatrical iron spiral staircase.
culture:Musée Gustave Moreau.text: The house-and-studio the Symbolist painter Gustave Moreau turned into his own museum, crammed with some 1,300 paintings, watercolours and drawings and reached by a theatrical iron spiral staircase. Late in life, Moreau decided his home should become a museum of his work, and had the upper floors rebuilt into vast top-lit studios linked by a swirling wrought-iron spiral stair — a stage set for his jewelled, mythological canvases. He died in 1898 and the museum opened in 1903, almost untouched since. It is one of Paris's great 'not-obvious' museums, hidden on a quiet 9th-arrondissement street. The real thing to grasp: the pictures are hung frame-to-frame, floor to ceiling, as Moreau intended — an overwhelming density you won't see in any conventional gallery. Signal Painter's own house-museum; opened 1903 with its famous spiral staircase

culture:Musée de la Chasse et de la Natu.name: Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature
culture:Musée de la Chasse et de la Natu.hook: A pair of Marais mansions turned into a witty, unsettling cabinet of curiosities on the human-animal relationship — taxidermy, arms, and contemporary art in panelled salons.
culture:Musée de la Chasse et de la Natu.text: A pair of Marais mansions turned into a witty, unsettling cabinet of curiosities on the human-animal relationship — taxidermy, arms, and contemporary art in panelled salons. It occupies the 17th-century Hôtel de Guénégaud — the only surviving private mansion built by architect François Mansart — and the neighbouring Hôtel de Mongelas, run by the Fondation François Sommer. Far from a dusty hunting collection, it stages animals and objects like an art installation — a room with a ceiling of owl feathers, a boar peering from a cabinet — which is why designers and art crowds treat it as a Marais secret. The real thing to know: it is a museum with a sense of humour and staging, closer to a Wunderkammer than a natural-history hall — and blessedly uncrowded. Signal In the Hôtel de Guénégaud, the only surviving private mansion by François Mansart; run by the Fondation François Sommer

culture:Musée Jacquemart-André.name: Musée Jacquemart-André
culture:Musée Jacquemart-André.hook: A Second-Empire mansion kept as its owners left it — a private house stuffed with Italian Renaissance masters, a rococo double staircase, and a frescoed tea room.
culture:Musée Jacquemart-André.text: A Second-Empire mansion kept as its owners left it — a private house stuffed with Italian Renaissance masters, a rococo double staircase, and a frescoed tea room. It was the home of banker Édouard André and the society painter Nélie Jacquemart — who first met him by painting his portrait, then married him — and together they filled it with Botticelli, Uccello and Tiepolo on annual buying trips to Italy. Bequeathed to the Institut de France, it reopened on 6 September 2024 after a €6.5-million restoration. This is the open, near-identical companion to the Camondo house nearby (see below): a plutocrat's private collection frozen in place. The real thing: don't skip the café — the tea room 'Le Nélie', in the former dining room, sits under a genuine Tiepolo ceiling. Signal Home of Édouard André & Nélie Jacquemart; reopened 6 September 2024 after €6.5M restoration

culture:Musée Nissim de Camondo.name: Musée Nissim de Camondo
culture:Musée Nissim de Camondo.hook: A 1910s mansion built as a shrine to 18th-century French decorative arts — and, unavoidably, to one family's annihilation.
culture:Musée Nissim de Camondo.text: A 1910s mansion built as a shrine to 18th-century French decorative arts — and, unavoidably, to one family's annihilation. Count Moïse de Camondo, from a great Sephardic banking family, built this house (1911–14) modelled on the Petit Trianon to hold his Marie-Antoinette-era furniture and Sèvres. He named it for his son Nissim, a French airman killed in 1917, and left it to the nation as a museum, opened in 1936. Years later his daughter Béatrice, her ex-husband and their two children were deported and murdered at Auschwitz — the family ended entirely. HONEST FLAG: the museum has been closed for renovation since 4 August 2024 and is announced to reopen only in early 2027, so it cannot be visited in 2026 — hold it for a return trip, and take Jacquemart-André (above) instead for now. Signal Opened 1936; CLOSED for renovation since 4 August 2024, reopening announced early 2027 — not visitable in 2026

culture:Galerie Vivienne & Passage des P.name: Galerie Vivienne & Passage des Panoramas
culture:Galerie Vivienne & Passage des P.hook: Two of Paris's surviving 19th-century glass-roofed shopping arcades — mosaic-floored Vivienne and the older, scruffier Panoramas — a few minutes apart.
culture:Galerie Vivienne & Passage des P.text: Two of Paris's surviving 19th-century glass-roofed shopping arcades — mosaic-floored Vivienne and the older, scruffier Panoramas — a few minutes apart. The covered passages were the ancestors of the department store: gaslit, weatherproof lanes of shops built when the streets were mud. The Passage des Panoramas is among the oldest, cut through in 1799 by an American shipowner, James Thayer, to link two rotundas showing 'panorama' paintings — and in 1817 it became the first Paris passage to be lit by gas. Galerie Vivienne (built 1823, opened 1826) is the grand one, a neo-classical arcade of mosaic floors and half-moon windows, still holding a famous antiquarian bookshop and old-world shopfronts. The real thing: of the dozens that once existed only about twenty remain — these two, walkable together, are the pair to see. Signal Passage des Panoramas cut through 1799 (gas-lit from 1817); Galerie Vivienne built 1823

hotel-bars:Bar Hemingway, Ritz Paris.name: Bar Hemingway, Ritz Paris
hotel-bars:Bar Hemingway, Ritz Paris.hook: A tiny wood-panelled cocktail room at the back of the Ritz, hung with the writer's photographs, where the martini is treated as scripture.
hotel-bars:Bar Hemingway, Ritz Paris.text: A tiny wood-panelled cocktail room at the back of the Ritz, hung with the writer's photographs, where the martini is treated as scripture. The room's history dates to 1921 and it passed through several names — Le Petit Bar, Bar Bertin — before taking Hemingway's, after the legend that he 'liberated' the German-occupied Ritz in 1944 by marching in and running up a tab for fifty-one dry martinis. It went dark in 1982 and stayed shut twelve years, reopening in 1994 under head barman Colin Field, whom Forbes once called the best bartender alive; he built its reputation on cocktails mixed to your mood, not a menu. The one real thing to know: it is tiny — around twenty-five seats, no reservations, arrive at opening (6pm) or queue. Signal Room dates to 1921; reopened 1994 under Colin Field (still head barman in 2026)

hotel-bars:Le Bar du Bristol.name: Le Bar du Bristol
hotel-bars:Le Bar du Bristol.hook: A jewel-box corner bar in Le Bristol designed as a cabinet of curiosities, where cocktails come with petits fours and, on weekend nights, a DJ.
hotel-bars:Le Bar du Bristol.text: A jewel-box corner bar in Le Bristol designed as a cabinet of curiosities, where cocktails come with petits fours and, on weekend nights, a DJ. Le Bristol opened in April 1925 on the Faubourg Saint-Honoré, the street of the Élysée Palace and the couture houses, and has always drawn a diplomatic-and-fashion crowd. The bar as it stands is comparatively young — inaugurated in 2012 — and was styled to feel like a collector's study rather than a hotel lounge, all curiosities and low light, with contemporary-art video playing behind the bar. The thing worth knowing: it is quietly one of the few grand-hotel bars in Paris with a genuine late crowd and music (its weekend 'Bristol After Dark' sets), not just hushed reverence. Signal Hotel opened April 1925; bar inaugurated 2012

hotel-bars:Bar de l'Hôtel Costes.name: Bar de l'Hôtel Costes
hotel-bars:Bar de l'Hôtel Costes.hook: The velvet-swathed, oxblood-and-gilt bar-and-courtyard of the Costes brothers' hotel — the Paris room that launched a thousand lounge compilations.
hotel-bars:Bar de l'Hôtel Costes.text: The velvet-swathed, oxblood-and-gilt bar-and-courtyard of the Costes brothers' hotel — the Paris room that launched a thousand lounge compilations. The Costes brothers, Jean-Louis and Gilbert, opened the hotel in 1995 and handed the interiors to Jacques Garcia, who dressed it in Napoleon III opulence — swags, deep reds, candlelight — that became the template for 'moody hotel glamour' worldwide. Its real legacy is sound: Stéphane Pompougnac, whose first job here was as a waiter in the courtyard café, was made resident DJ and mixed the 'Hôtel Costes' compilation series (running to its fifteenth volume in 2011), one of the first hotels anywhere to commission its own soundtrack. Know this: it is a scene, priced and posed accordingly — come for the room and the sound, not a bargain. Signal Opened 1995; Jacques Garcia interiors, home of the Costes compilations (Vols 1–15, 1999–2011)

hotel-bars:Bar Joséphine, Hôtel Lutetia.name: Bar Joséphine, Hôtel Lutetia
hotel-bars:Bar Joséphine, Hôtel Lutetia.hook: The frescoed grand bar of the Left Bank's only 'Palace'-distinction hotel, named for Josephine Baker, with regular live jazz.
hotel-bars:Bar Joséphine, Hôtel Lutetia.text: The frescoed grand bar of the Left Bank's only 'Palace'-distinction hotel, named for Josephine Baker, with regular live jazz. The Lutetia opened in 1910, built by the owners of Le Bon Marché to lodge their department-store clients — the first luxury hotel on the Left Bank, later a haunt of Picasso, Joyce and Saint-Exupéry, and in 2019 the only Left Bank hotel to win France's official 'Palace' label. During the 2014–2018 restoration, workers uncovered the bar's original 1910 ceiling-and-wall frescoes by Adrien Karbowsky, hidden for decades under coats of paint and a veil of white-painted glass; they were painstakingly brought back over roughly 17,000 hours. The one real thing: it earns its name honestly with a strong jazz programme, so time a visit to a live set. Signal 1910 hotel; Karbowsky frescoes found under paint and painted glass, restored by 2018; Left Bank's only Palace (2019)

walks:Coulée verte René-Dumont (Promenad.name: Coulée verte René-Dumont (Promenade Plantée)
walks:Coulée verte René-Dumont (Promenad.hook: A 4.7 km green ribbon that runs from behind the Opéra Bastille to the edge of the Bois de Vincennes, the first stretch riding ten metres up on the brick arches of a dead railway viaduct (the vaults below are the Viaduc des Arts craft workshops). Rose arbours, bamboo, lavender, pergolas — and near silence above the traffic.
walks:Coulée verte René-Dumont (Promenad.text: A 4.7 km green ribbon that runs from behind the Opéra Bastille to the edge of the Bois de Vincennes, the first stretch riding ten metres up on the brick arches of a dead railway viaduct (the vaults below are the Viaduc des Arts craft workshops). Rose arbours, bamboo, lavender, pergolas — and near silence above the traffic. The terroir here is a resurrected railway. Trains ran Bastille-to-Vincennes on this viaduct until 1969; when the line died, most cities would have demolished it. Instead landscape architect Jacques Vergely and architect Philippe Mathieux planted a garden along the top — the first project in the world to turn an elevated railway into an urban garden — and it opened in 1993. The one real thing to know, because everyone gets it backwards: this predates New York's High Line, which only opened in 2009, and its creators cite the Paris promenade as a precedent. Paris did it first. Signal Inaugurated 1993 — the first elevated railway turned into a park walkway (verified: Wikipedia, Secrets of Paris)

walks:Parc des Buttes-Chaumont.name: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont
walks:Parc des Buttes-Chaumont.hook: A dramatic, hilly park with a cliff-ringed lake, a suspension footbridge, and a miniature Roman temple perched on a crag — the Temple de la Sibylle — that gives the best free view over the east of Paris. Locals sprawl on the steep lawns; this is where the 19th actually suns itself.
walks:Parc des Buttes-Chaumont.text: A dramatic, hilly park with a cliff-ringed lake, a suspension footbridge, and a miniature Roman temple perched on a crag — the Temple de la Sibylle — that gives the best free view over the east of Paris. Locals sprawl on the steep lawns; this is where the 19th actually suns itself. The terroir is faked geology built on a cursed hill. This was the Gibbet of Montfaucon, where from the 13th century to 1760 the bodies of the hanged were displayed to rot; afterwards a refuse dump and a yard for cutting up horse carcasses. Napoleon III and engineer Adolphe Alphand turned the most reviled ground in Paris into a park for the new working-class districts — blasting the exhausted gypsum quarry into cliffs, trucking in topsoil, and topping the 50-metre crag with Gabriel Davioud's temple copied from the one at Tivoli. It opened for the 1867 Exposition Universelle. Signal Opened 1 April 1867; built on the medieval gibbet of Montfaucon and a spent gypsum quarry (verified: Wikipedia, napoleon.org)

walks:Cimetière du Père-Lachaise.name: Cimetière du Père-Lachaise
walks:Cimetière du Père-Lachaise.hook: The largest cemetery in Paris is also one of its great walks: 44 cobbled, chestnut-shaded hectares climbing a hillside, where you pass between cats, moss and the tombs of Chopin, Wilde, Piaf and Proust. Go for the upper avenues, not the celebrity graves — that's where Parisians actually stroll on a Sunday.
walks:Cimetière du Père-Lachaise.text: The largest cemetery in Paris is also one of its great walks: 44 cobbled, chestnut-shaded hectares climbing a hillside, where you pass between cats, moss and the tombs of Chopin, Wilde, Piaf and Proust. Go for the upper avenues, not the celebrity graves — that's where Parisians actually stroll on a Sunday. The terroir is a marketing trick that worked. When Napoleon opened it in 1804 on the old estate of Louis XIV's confessor (Père La Chaise — hence the name), Parisians refused to be buried so far from the city, and it drew barely any funerals. So in 1817 the administrators staged a stunt — they paraded in the supposed bones of Molière and La Fontaine, and the purported remains of the medieval lovers Héloïse and Abélard under a canopy of salvaged abbey stone. It worked cynically well: over 33,000 graves by 1830. The honest caveat the guides skip: none of those relics are secure — historians doubt La Fontaine's body ever left its first cemetery, and 'Héloïse & Abélard' are recorded only as 'purported' remains. Signal Opened 1804; jumpstarted in 1817 by relocating 'Molière, La Fontaine' and 'Héloïse & Abélard' (verified: Wikipedia, napoleon.org, Mental Floss)

walks:Parc Rives de Seine (the car-free.name: Parc Rives de Seine (the car-free quais)
walks:Parc Rives de Seine (the car-free.hook: The riverside expressway is gone. Both banks between the Musée d'Orsay and the Arsenal marina are now a car-free promenade — floating gardens planted on barges, café terraces, and stone steps down to the water where Parisians sit at dusk with a bottle.
walks:Parc Rives de Seine (the car-free.text: The riverside expressway is gone. Both banks between the Musée d'Orsay and the Arsenal marina are now a car-free promenade — floating gardens planted on barges, café terraces, and stone steps down to the water where Parisians sit at dusk with a bottle. The terroir is the Seine taken back from cars. For decades the Voie Georges-Pompidou was a motorway welded to the river; you physically could not reach the water. Mayor Delanoë pedestrianised the left bank in 2013 — with five gardens floated on barges, moored near the Pont de l'Alma — and Hidalgo seized the right bank in 2017, against furious driver opposition that went all the way to the courts. The one real thing: this is the newest great walk in Paris and the most contested one, a live argument about who the river belongs to. Signal Left bank pedestrianised 2013 (Delanoë), right bank 2017 (Hidalgo) (verified: Wikipedia, Paris je t'aime)

walks:Jardin du Palais-Royal.name: Jardin du Palais-Royal
walks:Jardin du Palais-Royal.hook: A perfect rectangle of clipped limes and rose beds enclosed by silent 18th-century arcades, hidden a block from the Louvre — with Daniel Buren's field of black-and-white striped columns in the forecourt. Office workers eat lunch on the fountain rim in near quiet.
walks:Jardin du Palais-Royal.text: A perfect rectangle of clipped limes and rose beds enclosed by silent 18th-century arcades, hidden a block from the Louvre — with Daniel Buren's field of black-and-white striped columns in the forecourt. Office workers eat lunch on the fountain rim in near quiet. The terroir is stillness on top of gunpowder. Cardinal Richelieu built the palace in the 1630s; a later Duc d'Orléans lined the garden with arcades of shops to clear his debts, and it became the pre-Revolutionary heart of Paris — cafés, gambling, radical pamphlets. It was here, at the Café de Foy, that Camille Desmoulins leapt onto a table on 12 July 1789 and called Paris to arms, two days before the Bastille fell. Colette wrote in an apartment above the garden until her death (the Allée Colette carries her name). In 1985–86, under Culture Minister Jack Lang, Daniel Buren filled the honour court with 260 candy-striped columns over the ventilation shafts — a national scandal then, a selfie shrine now. Signal Garden of Richelieu's 1630s palace; Buren's 'Les Deux Plateaux' (260 columns) installed 1985–86 under Jack Lang (verified: Secrets of Paris, fr.wikipedia)

walks:Place des Vosges.name: Place des Vosges
walks:Place des Vosges.hook: Thirty-six brick-and-stone pavilions over vaulted arcades, wrapped around a garden of four lawns and clipped limes — the oldest planned square in Paris and a model for the residential squares that spread across Europe after it.
walks:Place des Vosges.text: Thirty-six brick-and-stone pavilions over vaulted arcades, wrapped around a garden of four lawns and clipped limes — the oldest planned square in Paris and a model for the residential squares that spread across Europe after it. The terroir is an early experiment in planning the city. Henri IV built it 1605–1612 as the Place Royale, on the rubble of the Hôtel des Tournelles — the royal palace demolished after Henri II died there in 1559 from a jousting splinter driven through his eye. The insistence on near-identical façades — same brick, same stone, same steep slate roof — was a deliberate act of royal planning, the first such uniform square in France (Madrid's Plaza Mayor, begun 1590, is its rare earlier European cousin). It was renamed Place des Vosges in 1800 to honour the first département to pay the Revolution's taxes. Victor Hugo wrote at No. 6 (1832–48; now his free museum). The one real thing: shelter under the arcades in the rain — they were designed four centuries ago precisely so you could stroll and shop dry. Signal Completed 1612; the oldest planned square in Paris (verified: Wikipedia, Le Marais Mood)

walks:Canal Saint-Martin.name: Canal Saint-Martin
walks:Canal Saint-Martin.hook: A 4.5 km canal of iron footbridges and stepped double locks, its plane-tree quais the Sunday-evening living room of the 10th — Parisians sit on the stone edge with cheese, a baguette and a bottle while boats grind up through the locks.
walks:Canal Saint-Martin.text: A 4.5 km canal of iron footbridges and stepped double locks, its plane-tree quais the Sunday-evening living room of the 10th — Parisians sit on the stone edge with cheese, a baguette and a bottle while boats grind up through the locks. The terroir is the water that stopped killing Parisians. By 1802 the city drank from the same Seine it dumped its sewage into, and cholera and dysentery did the rest. Napoleon ordered a canal to pipe clean water in from the river Ourcq — and to pay for it the state taxed wine, so Parisians quite literally drank their way to clean water. It opened in 1825, four years after Napoleon died in exile. About half its length was later roofed over under Napoleon III (the tree-lined Boulevard Richard-Lenoir runs above the covered stretch). The one real thing: this is the anti-Seine — no monuments, barely a tour boat, just the neighbourhood at its own aperitif rituals. Signal Ordered by Napoleon in 1802, opened 1825, funded by a wine tax (verified: Wikipedia, Life in Rural France)

secret-gems:Square du Vert-Galant.name: Square du Vert-Galant
secret-gems:Square du Vert-Galant.hook: A small triangular garden at the very prow of the Île de la Cité, reached by stairs down from the Pont Neuf, sitting at the river's natural level — a weeping willow at the point, a few benches, and the Seine forking around you on three sides. Arguably the single best place in Paris to sit.
secret-gems:Square du Vert-Galant.text: A small triangular garden at the very prow of the Île de la Cité, reached by stairs down from the Pont Neuf, sitting at the river's natural level — a weeping willow at the point, a few benches, and the Seine forking around you on three sides. Arguably the single best place in Paris to sit. The terroir is medieval Paris, seven metres down. Most people cross the Pont Neuf above and never notice the stairs exist. The name honours Henri IV, the 'Vert-Galant' (green gallant — a wink at the ageing king's tireless string of mistresses), whose green-oxidised bronze statue rides on the bridge overhead. The one real thing to know: you're sitting at the original ground level of the old city, some seven metres below today's streets — the island was built up over the centuries. The square itself was made in 1884 by joining two silty islets to the Cité. Come at sunset; the willow and the splitting river are the whole point. Signal Created 1884; named for Henri IV, whose Pont Neuf was finished 1606 (inaugurated 1607) (verified: Wikipedia, Ville de Paris)

secret-gems:La Petite Ceinture.hook: The abandoned railway that once ringed all of Paris, now a chain of wild, sunken green corridors — rails still in the ballast, buddleia, brambles, even foxes — reopened in pieces. This is a rare central-Paris place that feels genuinely unmanicured: a ruin, not a garden.
secret-gems:La Petite Ceinture.text: The abandoned railway that once ringed all of Paris, now a chain of wild, sunken green corridors — rails still in the ballast, buddleia, brambles, even foxes — reopened in pieces. This is a rare central-Paris place that feels genuinely unmanicured: a ruin, not a garden. The terroir is the city's forgotten ring handed back to nature. Built from 1852 under the Second Empire to run freight and then passengers around the old walls, the Petite Ceinture was strangled by the new Métro after 1900 and closed to passengers in 1934 — then simply left. For decades nobody knew what to do with it, and the trench went feral: the 15th-arrondissement stretch alone now counts 200-plus wild plant species and 70 animal species over 1.5 km of old track. The one real thing to know: the longest continuous walk is in the 12th — about 1.6 km from rue de Charenton to avenue de Saint-Mandé, with a 200 m nature trail and a community garden. Go for the strangeness, not the polish. Signal Rail line closed to passengers 1934; nine sections walkable across nine arrondissements today (verified: Wikipedia, Ville de Paris, ASPCRF)
